sources.entry: Rules for Designing Precise Anki Cards

summary.title: Rules for Designing Precise Anki Cards
summary.one_liner: Learn how to write precise, single-answer, context-free spaced-repetition flashcards in Anki that test what you actually want to remember.
takeaways: Make each card ask exactly one thing, following the minimum information principle (split broad 'describe X' prompts into several specific questions).
Make sure each question permits exactly one correct answer; avoid 'give an example' prompts by inverting them into 'is X an example of Y' cloze cards.
Avoid enumeration cards and yes/no questions; ask 'why' or 'which' questions and learn the individual parts of a set through separate cards.
Make questions context-free by naming the topic at the start and not referencing a specific source like 'our book'.
Treat cards as editable: fix problems during review and use the 'mark' tag to revisit them later.
summary.summary: The article argues that spaced-repetition card quality matters most, since an SRS will efficiently memorize whatever a card asks, including irrelevant details. The author walks through rules with real examples from his Anki collection: ask exactly one thing, permit exactly one answer (avoid 'example' and vague prompts), avoid enumerations and yes/no questions, and keep questions context-free without source references. Each rule shows a bad card, explains the problem, and gives a rewritten version. It closes with advice to edit cards during review and use a 'marked' tag to fix them later. The piece references SuperMemo's Twenty Rules of Formulating Knowledge throughout.
